sections.html:
Summersville is the seat of Nicholas County, a central West Virginia county on the Allegheny Plateau, and Richwood is the other city. Population stood at 24,604 in 2020 and is estimated at 23,848 for 2025. Roughly 80.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and a typical home is worth $93,700.

Seven magisterial districts cover the county: Beaver, Grant, Hamilton, Jefferson, Kentucky, Summersville and Wilderness. Census-designated places include Belva, Craigsville, Fenwick, Nettie and Tioga. Sellers here may hold a house in Summersville or Richwood, a rural parcel or an inherited home, and tourism around Summersville Lake and the Gauley River keeps some rental and vacation properties in the mix.

Two elected offices split the work. The Sheriff's Tax Office takes your money, while the Assessor decides what the property is worth.

OfficeWherePhone
Sheriff's Tax Office700 Main Street, Summersville, WV 26651; online record search and payment304-872-7842
Assessor700 Main Street, Suite 4304-872-7800
County CommissionCourthouse complex304-872-7830

The assessor's page lists these dates: the homestead exemption request is due December 1, the assessment year begins July 1, and the farm report is due September 1. If you are unsure which of these concerns you, a phone call to the assessor settles it.

Nicholas County bills run on the statewide calendar. Expect a ticket from July 15 onward, with one half due September 1 and the other March 1.

  • Paying ahead of either date takes 2.5 percent off.
  • Delinquency begins October 1 for a first half left unpaid.
  • A second half left unpaid turns delinquent April 1.
  • From delinquency onward, interest accrues at 9 percent annually.

A parcel still behind on September 1 lands on a second list, which the sheriff builds by September 10. Any lien still open goes to the State Auditor on October 31. Redeeming before then means paying the tax, interest and charges, and the charges include $25 for the list plus $10 for every mailed notice.

sections.h2: How much of the bill goes to schools?
sections.html:
About two thirds of the 2024 levy went to schools. The state's tax year 2024 publication shows $17,865,512 levied across all purposes: $11,790,823 for schools, $4,881,552 for county purposes, $1,107,795 for municipal purposes and $85,342 for the state.

The real estate portion was $10,024,686. Owner-occupied residential property (Class II) made up $4,777,644 of it. Property outside towns (Class III) brought in $3,104,634, and property inside towns (Class IV) $2,142,409. The state says the Class II rate is twice Class I and Classes III and IV are four times Class I, so an empty or rented house in Summersville or Richwood pays at a higher rate than the same house lived in by its owner.

Begin by speaking with the assessor. If that fails, present your case when the county commission meets as the board of equalization and review.

State law has the commissioners sit as the board by February 1. Adjourning is allowed after February 15, and the work must end with the month. Errors get fixed there, and a value above or below 60 percent of market is reset to 60 percent. Raising a value takes five days of written notice. An owner who stays away loses that year's correction, other than by going to the Office of Tax Appeals. A dispute over class or taxability is outside the board's reach and goes through a protest to the assessor.

Sellers in Summersville, Richwood or the rural districts can prepare in a few quick moves. Get from the sheriff a year-by-year balance, fire fee included. Ask the assessor which class your property carries and whether the homestead exemption is on file, since the Class II rate is half the rate for other real estate. Check the district name on your ticket against what the assessor shows. Pass the results to the title company so closing numbers come out right.

A house that has sat vacant may have been billed at the higher rate, so it is worth asking about class before you tell a buyer what the yearly tax will be. If the property came to you through a will, bring the paperwork showing how title passed, because the exemption changes with the next July 1 after a transfer.

Take $20,000 off assessed value if you live in the home and are 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled. The owner must have lived in the state for two consecutive calendar years, though returning residents and military retirees have exceptions.

Whoever owns the home on the July 1 assessment date holds it. A deed or will moving the house ends it at the next July 1 unless the new owner qualifies, which means a March sale leaves the old owner's exemption in place until the following July.

The buyer's title company will look for unpaid tickets, so deal with them first. Start with the Sheriff's Tax Office and ask for the balance on each tax year, including fire fee charges, which the office's online system lists.

Filing the deed at the clerk's office brings a transfer tax. The base is $1.10 per $500 of value (the county keeps it as of July 1, 2025). A county charge of 55 cents per $500 rides on top unless the commission changed it, and a $20 fee is added. Sellers normally pay, though a buyer may accept the deed with the tax unpaid.

  1. Ask the sheriff what is owed for each tax year.
  2. Pass those figures to the title company, which pays them out of proceeds.
  3. Have the deed recorded at the clerk's office once closing is done.

A seller who owns a house with several years open, or whose heirs have not yet been added to the deed, should start these steps early. Fire fee charges can sit on the ticket alongside property tax, so ask the sheriff's office to include them in the payoff. Bring a photo ID and the latest ticket when you visit the courthouse in Summersville.

Summersville Lake and the lower Gauley bring a rafting season each fall, and vacation rentals, campgrounds and boat rentals serve the visitors. An owner with a cabin or a house let to guests should ask the assessor how it is classed. Because the state taxes rented real estate at four times the Class I rate, a rental can carry a heavier ticket than a neighbor's owner-occupied house, and a buyer pricing the property will notice that difference. Pulling the ticket history from the sheriff's online record search before you list shows exactly what has been billed.

High water has hit this county before. A deadly 2016 flood on the Cherry River devastated Richwood and other places in the county, so a Richwood address will draw questions from buyers and insurers about flood history.

Water damage, put-off repairs and an unsettled estate are all fine for a cash buyer who takes the house as-is. The title company clears open tax from your proceeds, and there are no repairs or open houses to arrange.

faqs.q: When are Nicholas County property taxes due?
faqs.a: One payment falls on September 1 and the other on March 1, and each earns a 2.5 percent discount when paid early. An unpaid half is delinquent from October 1 or April 1.

faqs.q: Where is the Nicholas County Sheriff's Tax Office?
faqs.a: It is at 700 Main Street in Summersville, WV 26651, and the phone number is 304-872-7842. The sheriff's system offers online tax search, online payment and fire fee inquiry.

faqs.q: What is the homestead exemption deadline in Nicholas County?
faqs.a: Requests are due December 1. It removes $20,000 of assessed value for qualifying owners aged 65 and up or permanently and totally disabled.

faqs.q: Do I still owe tax if I sell mid-year?
faqs.a: Yes, for anything unpaid. That year's tax attaches to the property as a lien, so any open ticket must be cleared by closing. The sheriff's office can give the balance, and the title company will confirm it.

faqs.q: How is a Nicholas County home assessed?
faqs.a: At 60 percent of market value, with the class setting the rate. Owner-occupied homes are Class II, taxed at twice the Class I rate, and other real estate in or outside municipalities is taxed at four times Class I.
